q-105298:
We take the derivative of each term and then add them, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ln⁡x-5csc⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}-5(-csc⁡xcot⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}+5csc⁡xcot⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}+5csc⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})cot⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }+5\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

q-1913:
We calculate the derivative using the product rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2{x}^{4}cot⁡x) \\  & =(-8{x}^{3})(cot⁡x)+(-2{x}^{4})(-{csc}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-8{x}^{3}cot⁡x+2{x}^{4}{csc}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-105314:
We calculate the derivative using the product rule, as follows:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({5}^{x}sec⁡x) \\  & ={5}^{x}ln⁡5sec⁡x+{5}^{x}sec⁡xtan⁡x \\  & ={5}^{x}sec⁡x(ln⁡5+tan⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

q-70874:
First, we calculate the derivative using the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ln⁡x+3csc⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}+3(-csc⁡xcot⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}-3csc⁡xcot⁡x\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{3})}-3csc⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})cot⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }-3(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }-3(\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }-2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-1904:
First, we calculate the derivative using the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{d}{dx}(-{x}^{2}+5csc⁡x) \\  & =2\cdot (-x)+5(-csc⁡xcot⁡x) \\  & =-2x-5csc⁡xcot⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into the derivative and get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =-2(\frac{\pi }{6})-5csc⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})cot⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3}-5\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{3} \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3}-10\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-113907:
Recall that

$$
\int sin⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =-cos⁡\theta +C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int (-6sin⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & =-6\int sin⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-6(-cos⁡\theta )+C \\  & =6cos⁡\theta +C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-2161:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int sin⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-cos⁡x+C, \\ \int cos⁡x\,\text{d}x & =sin⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (cos⁡x-sin⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int cos⁡x\,\text{d}x-\int sin⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =sin⁡x-(-cos⁡x)+C \\  & =sin⁡x+cos⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-2038:
Recall that

$$
\int sec⁡\theta tan⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =sec⁡\theta +C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int (-sec⁡\theta tan⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta  & =-\int sec⁡\theta tan⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-(sec⁡\theta )+C \\  & =-sec⁡\theta +C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-113920:
Recall that

$$
\int csc⁡xcot⁡x\,\text{d}x=-csc⁡x+C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int -3csc⁡x\,cot⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-3\int csc⁡xcot⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3(-csc⁡x)+C \\  & =3csc⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-113936:
Recall that 

$$
\int {sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =tan⁡\theta +C
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int 2{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =2\int {sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2tan⁡\theta +C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-49122:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int sec⁡xtan⁡x\,\text{d}x & =sec⁡x+C, \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =tan⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int sec⁡x(7sec⁡x+4tan⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int (7{sec}^{2}⁡x+4sec⁡xtan⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int 7{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int 4sec⁡xtan⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =7\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x+4\int sec⁡xtan⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =7tan⁡x+4sec⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-71664:
Recall that 

$$
\int {csc}^{2}⁡y\,\text{d}y=-cot⁡y+C
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int -{csc}^{2}⁡y\,\text{d}y & =-\int {csc}^{2}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =-(-cot⁡y)+C \\  & =cot⁡y+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-71663:
Recall that 

$$
\int {csc}^{2}⁡y\,\text{d}y=-cot⁡y+C
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int -3{csc}^{2}⁡y\,\text{d}y & =-3\int {csc}^{2}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3(-cot⁡y)+C \\  & =3cot⁡y+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-70359:
In this case, we need to put the fractions over a common denominator of $x(2x-1),$ since there are no common factors in either denominator that we can exploit. 

To do this, we multiply the top and bottom of the first fraction by $x,$ and the top and bottom of the second fraction by $2x-1:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{2x-1}-\frac{3}{x} & = \\ \frac{x}{x}\cdot \frac{6}{2x-1}-\frac{2x-1}{2x-1}\cdot \frac{3}{x} & = \\ \frac{6x}{x(2x-1)}-\frac{3(2x-1)}{x(2x-1)} & = \\ \frac{6x-3(2x-1)}{x(2x-1)} & = \\ \frac{6x-6x+3}{x(2x-1)} & = \\ \frac{3}{x(2x-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

q-113219:
Using the fact that $5=\frac{5}{1},$ we can write the expression as

$$
\frac{5}{1}+\frac{h-3}{h}.
$$

 

In order to add the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. So, we put both fractions over a common denominator of $h$ by multiplying the top and bottom of the first fraction by $h:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{1}+\frac{h-3}{h} & = \\ \frac{h}{h}\cdot \frac{5}{1}+\frac{h-3}{h} & = \\ \frac{5h}{h}+\frac{h-3}{h}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we add the fractions and simplify the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5h}{h}+\frac{h-3}{h} & = \\ \frac{5h+h-3}{h} & = \\ \frac{6h-3}{h} & = \\ \frac{3(2h-1)}{h}\end{aligned}
$$

q-119308:
**Method 1**

To plot $y=-f(x)+4,$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x)-1.$

- Then, we shift the graph vertically by $1$ unit up and get the graph of $y=f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(2,3)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(2,3+1)=(2,4).
$$

- Next, we reflect the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(2,4)$ will be mapped  to the point

$$
(2,-(4))=(2,-4).
$$

- Finally, shift the result vertically by $4$ units up and obtain the graph of $y=-f(x)+4.$ After this transformation, the point $(2,-4)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(2,-4+4)=(2,0).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(2,3)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x)-1$, we have that 

$$
f(2)-1=3\,⟹\,f(2)=4.
$$

Now consider the graph of $y=-f(x)+4.$ Substituting $x=2$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-f(2)+4 \\  & =-4+4 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(2,0)$ must lie on $y=-f(x)+4.$
